title: What even is AI?
blurb: Cut through the hype — what AI really is, where you already use it, and why it's not magic.

steps.title: AI is everywhere — but what *is* it?
steps.body:
You've heard "AI" a hundred times. It unlocks your phone with your face, suggests the next video, finishes your sentences.

But here's a secret: almost nobody can explain what it actually **is**. By the end of this lesson, you will — and you'll even train a tiny one yourself.

steps.title: The one-sentence answer
steps.body:
**AI is a computer program that learns from examples instead of being told exactly what to do.**

Normal programs follow rules a human wrote: "if the light is red, stop." An AI is different — you show it **lots of examples**, and it figures out the pattern on its own.

steps.title: An example you already get
steps.body:
Imagine teaching a little kid the difference between a cat and a dog. You don't hand them a rulebook. You just point at animals: *"cat… dog… cat… dog…"*

After enough examples, the kid just **knows**. AI learns the exact same way — from examples, not rules.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.question: What's the big difference between AI and a normal computer program?
choices: AI learns patterns from examples instead of following written rules
steps.explain: That's it — AI learns the pattern from examples. A normal program just follows rules a person wrote out.

steps.title: What AI is NOT
steps.body:
Let's bust three myths right now:

- ❌ **It's not magic.** It's math and examples — a lot of them.
- ❌ **It's not a person.** It doesn't *understand* or *feel* anything. It finds patterns.
- ❌ **It's not always right.** It can be confidently wrong (you'll see why soon).

steps.title: Myth check
steps.question: True or false: an AI *understands* the world the way a human does.
steps.explain: False! AI is a brilliant **pattern-spotter**, but it doesn't understand meaning like you do. That's an important difference to remember.

steps.title: How learning actually works
steps.body:
Every AI does three things:

1. **See examples** (lots of cat and dog photos)
2. **Find the pattern** (cats have pointy ears, dogs are bigger…)
3. **Make a guess** on something new ("that's probably a cat")

More examples → better patterns → better guesses. Simple as that.

steps.title: Where you already meet AI
steps.body:
You use AI all day without noticing:

- 📷 Your photos app finding every picture of your dog
- 🎵 "Songs you might like"
- 🗣️ Voice assistants understanding what you said
- ✍️ Autocorrect and text suggestions

Each one learned from millions of examples.

steps.title: Spot the AI
steps.question: Which of these most likely uses AI?
choices: A light switch turning on a bulb
Your phone recognizing your face to unlock
steps.explain: Face unlock learned from many face examples — that's AI. The others just follow fixed rules.

steps.title: Why AI gets things wrong
steps.body:
An AI is only as good as the examples it learned from.

If it only ever saw small dogs, it might call a *horse* a dog. It didn't "think" wrong — it just never saw the right examples. **Garbage in, garbage out.** Keep this idea in your pocket; it explains almost every AI mistake.

steps.title: Why the mistake?
steps.question: An AI keeps calling a wolf a "dog." What's the most likely reason?
choices: It never learned from enough wolf examples
Wolves and dogs are the same
steps.explain: Right — it learned from dog examples and never really saw wolves, so it guesses the closest thing it knows.

steps.title: Your turn — teach a real one
steps.body:
Enough talk. You're going to **train an actual AI** right now, in your browser, using your camera.

Pick two things to tell apart, show it a few examples of each, and watch it learn. This is the exact same idea behind the biggest AI systems in the world — just smaller.

steps.title: Train a tiny AI
steps.body: Add a few example photos of two different things (like ✌️ vs 👍), then press **Train it!** and test it live.

steps.title: What you just did
steps.body:
You showed an AI examples, it found the pattern, and it made guesses. **That's the whole game** — whether it's your tiny classifier or a giant model that writes essays.

The big ones just have *way* more examples and *way* more computing power. The core idea is identical.

steps.title: Lock it in
steps.question: What's the single most important ingredient for teaching an AI?
steps.explain: Examples are everything. Good, plentiful, balanced examples make a smart AI — which is exactly what the next lesson is all about: **data**.

steps.title: What you learned 🎉
steps.body:
- AI **learns from examples**, not written rules
- It's a pattern-spotter — **not magic, not a person, not always right**
- It gets things wrong when its examples were missing or unfair
- You **trained a real one yourself!**

**Next up:** where all those examples come from — *data* — and why good data is the secret to good AI.
